claims.overstatement: One phrase goes beyond the source: the claim says that with alcohol present 'less benzoylecgonine ... was formed and excreted'. What the paper shows is a lower peak plasma level (452 against 652 ng/ml, P < 0.01) and lower urinary output (concentration 7,770 against 14,800 ng/ml, P < 0.02; amount in 24 h 18.5 against 31.3 million ng, P < 0.01), while the plasma area under the curve did not differ (6,050 against 6,300 h·ng/ml, not significant). The authors say in the Discussion that comparable areas under the curve suggest similar amounts were formed in both conditions, and that the pattern could instead reflect slower elimination with alcohol present. 'Less formed' is the authors' expectation, not their result; 'less excreted' is supported. Everything else from this source checks out as worded, including the unblinded, non-randomized cocaine-alone session in 6 of the 10 people 1-3 months later and the labelled cocaethylene tracer given in every session. Editors' calculations recomputed: 452/652 = 69%; 7,770/14,800 = 53% (the paper's text says 52%).
claims.note: Sample qualification the claim does not carry: these 10 people were not dependent by DSM-IV criteria on any drug other than nicotine, intravenous use was the preferred route for all of them, and most also used tobacco, cannabis or other drugs. A second qualification: the 7.5 mg labelled cocaethylene tracer reached higher plasma peaks than the cocaethylene formed from cocaine (84.7 and 67.7 ng/ml in the two 1.2 mg/kg conditions), and the authors say its levels were higher than expected and may have partly obscured differences between conditions.

anchors.page: printed p. 170 (PDF p. 2); printed p. 171 (PDF p. 3)
anchors.extracted: Double-blind, balanced crossover, five treatments in 10 people: oral alcohol 1 g/kg with labelled cocaine at 0.3, 0.6 or 1.2 mg/kg, alcohol with cocaine placebo, and double placebo (study conditions). Cocaine was infused intravenously over 15 minutes at a constant rate, starting 1 hour after the first drink; 7.5 mg of differently labelled cocaethylene was infused at the same time in every session as a tracer. Six of the ten returned 1-3 months later for cocaine 1.2 mg/kg with placebo alcohol; that session was neither blinded nor randomized (stated in 4.1 Study limitations, printed p. 180).

8 men and 2 women, mean age 34 (SD 7), mean weight 71 kg (SD 7). All had used cocaine and alcohol, typically around the same time, and none was dependent by DSM-IV criteria on drugs other than nicotine; none had ever sought treatment for cocaine-related problems. The preferred route for all was intravenous. Most also used tobacco (7 of 10), cannabis (8), amphetamines (3), heroin (3) or diazepam (1).

anchors.locator: 3.2.5 Fractional conversion of cocaine to cocaethylene
anchors.extracted: For every 10 mg of labelled cocaine given, a mean of 1.8 mg of cocaethylene was formed (range 1.0-4.0), a fractional conversion of 17% (SD 6) after correction for molecular weight; conversion did not differ significantly between the three cocaine doses.

anchors.page: printed p. 175 (PDF p. 7); printed p. 174 (PDF p. 6)
anchors.extracted: Cocaethylene peak concentrations 16.8 (SD 7.64), 30.1 (11.1) and 53.1 (15.0) ng/ml at the three cocaine doses, against cocaine peaks of 250 (73.0), 438 (151) and 891 (271) ng/ml. Time to peak 1.31, 1.33 and 1.55 h for cocaethylene against 0.31, 0.36 and 0.28 h for cocaine; half-life 2.61, 2.62 and 2.47 h for cocaethylene against 1.82, 1.60 and 1.77 h for cocaine. Both tables note that no assayable concentrations were detected in the double-placebo and alcohol-plus-cocaine-placebo conditions.

anchors.locator: 3.2.7 Cocaine plus ethanol versus cocaine administered alone; Table 4 (printed p. 176, n = 6)
anchors.extracted: In the 6 people tested both ways at 1.2 mg/kg: cocaine area under the curve 1,030 (SD 145) against 1,010 (227) h·ng/ml and peak 968 (298) against 823 (203) ng/ml, neither significantly different; cocaine half-life 1.91 (0.51) against 1.29 (0.15) h, P < 0.02. Peak plasma benzoylecgonine 452 (62.2) against 652 (111) ng/ml, P < 0.01 (the text calls this 69% of the cocaine-alone value); benzoylecgonine area under the curve 6,050 (1,890) against 6,300 (1,540), not significant; urine benzoylecgonine concentration 7,770 (3,550) against 14,800 (7,620) ng/ml, P < 0.02, and amount excreted in 24 h 18.5 against 31.3 million ng, P < 0.01. No assayable formed cocaethylene was found in the cocaine-only condition.

anchors.locator: 4. Discussion, 3rd paragraph (beginning 'Ethanol inhibits the methylesterase hydrolysis')
anchors.extracted: The authors state that comparable plasma benzoylecgonine areas under the curve suggest similar amounts were formed in both 1.2 mg/kg conditions, and that the comparable values might instead be explained by less formation together with slower elimination when alcohol is present. This qualifies the claim's 'less benzoylecgonine was formed'.

anchors.page: printed p. 178 (PDF p. 10); printed p. 179 (PDF p. 11)
anchors.locator: 3.3.1.2 Cocaine plus ethanol versus cocaine alone; 3.3.2.2 Cocaine plus ethanol versus cocaine alone
anchors.extracted: In the 6 people tested both ways, heart rate was higher across time with alcohol than with cocaine alone (P < 0.05) but not at its peak; systolic and diastolic blood pressure and rate-pressure product did not differ across time or at peak. Total intoxication across time was higher with alcohol (P < 0.02) and drug liking across time was higher (P < 0.04), while peak ratings did not differ.

anchors.page: printed p. 179 (PDF p. 11); printed p. 180 (PDF p. 12)
anchors.locator: 4. Discussion, 6th paragraph; 4.1 Study limitations and possible pitfalls
anchors.extracted: Unlike five earlier studies that gave cocaine nasally, this study found no rise in cocaine peak concentration or area under the curve when alcohol was added; the authors put this down to the intravenous route, which avoids alcohol's effect on nasal absorption. Limitations they state: the final cocaine-alone session was neither blinded nor randomized; only one alcohol dose was used; the 15-minute infusion may have blunted peak subjective effects; the small sample and large variability may have hidden differences; and the labelled cocaethylene tracer reached higher levels than expected and may have partly obscured differences between conditions.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of this source. Two small points. The paper's sentence on breath alcohol reads 'in all the experimental conditions'; the claim's 'in every session with alcohol' is the sensible reading, since the placebo sessions contained no alcohol. The '5 minutes before the infusion began' is the paper's own framing of the 55-minute peak, stated for breath alcohol concentrations in 3.2.6; the ratings of alcohol intoxication are reported with the same 55-minute peak in 3.3.2.1. The claim is careful to say the study reports no rating of drunkenness separate from the alcohol-intoxication rating, which is right: the three verbal 0-100 scales were ethanol intoxication, cocaine intoxication and total intoxication.
claims.note: Design point in the claim's favour: because the alcohol was drunk an hour before the cocaine, the authors themselves say the absence of a difference in peak alcohol levels and effects is what the design would be expected to produce. No observer rating of apparent drunkenness and no driving measure appear anywhere in the paper.

anchors.extracted: Ethanol intoxication peaked 55 minutes after the beginning of alcohol administration, and ethanol intoxication ratings did not differ between treatments, that is whatever cocaine dose or cocaine placebo followed. In the same subsection, cocaine and total intoxication ratings across time were greater in every cocaine condition than with alcohol alone (P < 0.05), rising with cocaine dose.

anchors.locator: 3.2.6 Breath ethanol concentrations (paragraph starts on printed p. 173 and continues on p. 177)
anchors.extracted: Breath alcohol peaked 55 minutes after the start of drinking, 5 minutes before the cocaine infusion began; the mean peak reached at least 0.12 g/dl (SD 0.014) in all the experimental conditions.

Participants rated, verbally on three 0-100 scales, their intoxication from alcohol, their intoxication from cocaine, and their total intoxication (a global feeling of intoxication from all drugs given), with 0 no drug effect and 100 the highest level ever experienced. Ratings were made before alcohol, at 40 and 55 minutes after it, and then at the times of the physiological measures. No rating of how drunk a person appeared to anyone else was taken.

The authors state that the absence of a difference in peak alcohol levels and effects when cocaine was added is what would be expected when alcohol is given an hour beforehand, so that peak levels and effects are reached before the cocaine arrives; they note one earlier study that also found no difference in blood alcohol or ratings of alcohol intoxication when cocaine was given before alcohol.

anchors.locator: 3.3.2.2 Cocaine plus ethanol versus cocaine alone
anchors.extracted: In the 6 people who had both sessions, total intoxication across time was higher with alcohol than with cocaine alone (P < 0.02) and drug liking across time was higher (P < 0.04); peak cocaine and total intoxication and peak good-drug-effect ratings did not differ. That cocaine-alone session was unblinded.
